title: Microfluidic Picoliter Bioreactor for Microbial Single-cell Analysis: Fabrication, System Setup, and Operation
protocol: Design the microfluidic device using CAD software.
Create a lithography photomask with electron beam writing.
Clean a 4 in silicon wafer with piranha solution.
Rinse the cleaned wafer with deionized water.
Dehydrate the wafer for 20 min at 200 °C.
Spin coat 1 µm SU-8 2000.5 photoresist onto the wafer.
Place the coated wafer on a hotplate to drive off excess solvent.
Insert 1st layer photomask with trapping regions of picoliter reactors into the mask aligner.
Expose wafer to 350-400 nm light (vacuum contact, 64 mJ/cm², t = 3 sec, I = 7 mW/cm²).
Perform post exposure bake on a hotplate at 95 °C (1 min at 65 °C, 1 min at 95 °C, and 1 min at 65 °C).
Place the wafer in a SU-8 developer bath for 1 minute.
Transfer the wafer into a second container with fresh SU-8 developer for few seconds.
Rinse the wafer in isopropanol to remove SU-8 developer.
Dry the wafer using nitrogen flow from a wafer spinner.
Hard bake the wafer for 10 minutes at 150 °C.
Spin coat 9 µm SU-8 2010 photoresist onto the wafer (dispense 4 ml resist, spin 10 sec with v = 500 rpm and a = 100 rpm/sec, then spin 30 s with v = 4,000 rpm and a = 300 rpm/sec).
Place the wafer on a hotplate at 95 °C to drive off excess solvent (15 min at 65 °C, 45-60 min at 95 °C, and 10 min at 65 °C).
Insert photomask with main channels for nutrient supply into the mask aligner.
Expose wafer to 350-400 nm light (hard contact, 64 mJ/cm², t = 10 sec, I = 7 mW/cm²).
Perform post exposure bake on a hotplate at 95 °C to finalize the polymerization of SU-8.
Place the wafer in a SU-8 developer bath for 45 sec.
Transfer the wafer into a second container with fresh SU-8 developer and develop for 60 sec.
Rinse the wafer 20 sec with isopropanol to remove any SU-8 developer residue.
Dry wafer using pressured nitrogen.
Hard bake the wafer at 150 °C.
Prepare a mixture of polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) base and curing agent in a 10:1 ratio.
Mix carefully until a homogenous solution is achieved which looks opaque.
Degas the PDMS mixture for approximately 30 min under slight vacuum until all bubbles have disappeared.
Prepare molding device with appropriate SU-8 wafer.
Pour PDMS mixture into the prepared device.
Bake the PDMS at 80 °C for 3 hours in the oven.
Peel off the PDMS slab from the wafer carefully.
Cut the PDMS slab into single chips using a clean and sharp scalpel.
Wash the chips in an n-pentane bath for 90 minutes.
Wash the chips with acetone for 90 minutes twice.
Dry the chips overnight to remove any solvent residue.
Punch inlet and outlet holes into the PDMS chip using a needle or hole puncher.
Clean the microfluidic PDMS chip carefully with isopropanol.
Remove dust particles on the structured PDMS side with scotch tape.
Clean a 170 µm thin glass slide with acetone.
Clean the glass slide with isopropanol successively.
Clean the glass slide finally with deionized water.
Dry the cleaned glass slide with pressurized nitrogen.
Warm up the plasma cleaner.
Run the plasma for approximately 300 seconds.
Plasma-oxidize glass slide and PDMS chip with power 50 W, time of 25 seconds, and oxygen flow rate of 20 sccm.
Align the PDMS and glass chip before bonding.
Place the PDMS chip carefully onto the glass slide.
Bake the final PDMS-glass chip for 10 seconds at 80 °C.
Prepare sterile filtered medium to prevent accumulation of undesired particles.
Inoculate one colony from an agar plate containing C. glutamicum ATCC 13032 into 20 ml of fresh BHI medium.
Incubate the inoculated BHI medium overnight (approximately 8-14 hours) at 30 °C on a rotary shaker (120 rpm).
Transfer 10 μl of the preculture into desired medium, such as CGXII21.
Let the cells grow overnight at 30 °C on a rotary shaker (120 rpm).
Transfer the desired amount of cell suspension into the medium for microfluidic cell cultivation.
Transfer 1 ml of bacterial culture into a sterile 2 ml tube immediately after assembling the PDMS chip.
Start microscope incubator 2 hrs before the experiment to warm-up the system.
Open incubator system and select the desired objective.
Add immersion oil onto the objective if required.
Mount the chip inside the chip holder.
Fix the glass plate with adhesive tape if necessary.
Center the sample on the microscope and focus onto the PLBR arrays.
Connect inlets and outlets with appropriate tubing.
Connect tubing to a waste reservoir.
Insert syringes into pumps and start media flow.
Rinse microfluidic channels with medium or buffer for approximately 1 hour.
Use a coating solution to coat channel walls if necessary.
For E. coli, use a 0.1% BSA solution to coat the channel walls.
For C. glutamicum, no coating is necessary.
Flush the chip with medium after the coating procedure.
Before cell seeding and cultivation, check for leaks and ensure constant temperature.
Make sure the desired bacteria solutions are available in appropriate syringes connected to tubing.
Disconnect buffer or coating solution and connect the cell suspension to the chip.
Change the complete needle as well as tubing to minimize death volume and air bubbles.
Infuse the cell suspension into the channels at a volumetric flow rate of 200 nl/min until most of the PLBRs are filled with cells.
Disconnect the cell suspension and connect the growth medium to the chip, ensuring no air bubble is introduced during the medium change.
Perfuse with fresh growth media at 100 nl/min.
Select specific PLBRs for time-lapse imaging that contain a single mother cell at the beginning of an experiment.
Choose appropriate frame rate depending on the number of PLBRs and microscope capacity.
Automatically close the shutter during stage movement and after each time-lapse measurement to prevent chromophore bleaching.
Configure the time-lapse microscopy sequence.
Start the experiment.
Stop the experiment after all PLBRs are overgrown.
Discard the microfluidic PDMS chip.
Determine PLBRs of interest where cultivation fulfills desired criteria.
Count the number of cells in each time frame to determine growth rate.
Plot time vs. ln (cell number) to calculate maximum growth rate.
Calculate the slope of the plot to represent the growth rate in [1/hr].
Analyze fluorescence data based on performed experiment.
